patches.value: E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx, the finite real Lebesgue integral, with exactly the normalization in the exercise (no factor 1/2).

Q has finite measure (2R)^n and C⊂int Q. All positive-order derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n∖C)×int J. The fields e,e_t and the products u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), j=1,...,n, are jointly continuous and zero outside C at interior times.

For every r∈int J, e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j∈{1,...,n}, ∂_{x_j}u(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u)(·,r) are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C and absolutely integrable on ℝ^n.

Discharge L1: F005 holds for every sequence of nonzero increments tending to zero and lying in |h|<η. This proves the full punctured limit as the increment tends to zero: otherwise one could choose, in successively smaller punctured neighborhoods of zero, increments whose energy quotients stay a fixed positive distance from ∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Such a sequence tends to zero and eventually lies in |h|<η, contradicting F005. Thus E is differentiable at t0 with E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0) dx. Together with F001, and generalization of arbitrary t0, this is N003. Neither the chosen support witnesses nor the test sequence escapes this conclusion.
